channel.description: Diagnostic feed grouped by acquisition connector.

item.title: Europe’s Banks Needn’t Race America Toward Crisis
item.description: If the European Union wants to compete better with America, there’s a long list of policy options it can pursue. Seeking to match the White House’s ambition in courting a banking crisis shouldn’t be among them.
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: Wildfires Followed by Floods May Leave Our Larders Bare
item.description: For many in the UK and Europe, the weather’s turn to cooler and showery this week will come as a welcome relief. But for farmers, it’ll be too little, too late after an unprecedented summer of heat, drought and fire.
item.dc:creator: Lara Williams

item.title: Fedorov’s Call for Ukraine Election Is Compelling and Wrong
item.description: Mykhailo Fedorov is perhaps the standout political figure to have been forged in Ukraine by Russia’s invasion. He is smart, young, so far untouched by any corruption scandal and the force behind two transformations that have proved critical to his nation’s survival: drone warfare and digital government. Even so, his demand this week for wartime presidential elections was reckless and wrong.
item.dc:creator: Marc Champion

item.title: Bessent’s Bond-Burner Wasn’t the Big Move He Hoped
item.description: Drastic changes in fiscal policy are needed, not signaling and symbols.
item.dc:creator: John Authers

item.title: Choking Iran's Economy Is the Least Bad Way to End the War
item.description: Over the years, I’ve witnessed at first-hand countries going literally broke under US economic pressure: Iraq, Venezuela and Cuba. The scenes I saw in Baghdad, Caracas and Havana were all very similar. The national currency became worthless, inflation skyrocketed and unemployment spiraled higher. And yet, American economic sanctions alone failed to force political change.
item.dc:creator: Javier Blas

item.title: GMO Mosquitoes and mRNA Vaccines Show Public Heath News Isn’t All Bad
item.description: Cancer vaccines, lower murder rates and other yelp-worthy public-health milestones.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Karl

item.title: Takaichi Can’t Rely on Foreign Policy Nostalgia
item.description: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has inherited a lot of things from her mentor, the late premier Shinzo Abe: Her support base, conservative credentials, and even her favored slogan of “Japan is back.”
item.dc:creator: Gearoid Reidy

item.title: Vietnam’s Hubris Risks Unraveling Its Economic Boom
item.description: Vietnam's economy is on a roll. Hanoi, basking in the kind of praise that Southeast Asian peers won prior to the region’s financial crisis in the 1990s, wants still more rapid growth. But leaders should be careful — such enthusiasm might well hasten the boom's undoing.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Moss

item.title: Treasury Buybacks Won’t Fix Soaring US Borrowing Costs
item.description: With the midterm elections less than three months away, President Donald Trump’s Treasury Department is starting to look desperate about the soaring cost to borrow. The Treasury said Wednesday it would increase its buybacks of longer-term government bonds “by at least double,” an amount analysts figure would bring purchases to $32 billion per quarter. Make no mistake about the motivations: 30-year bond yields this week hit their highest since 2007, pushing borrowing costs higher for the governme
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Levin

item.title: This Bad Movie Is a Good Guide to China’s Stock Market
item.description: Frustrated stock investors in China are finding dark humor from a crude, low-budget film that has become a box office hit.
item.dc:creator: Shuli Ren

item.title: Target Earnings: The ‘Target Run’ Is Making a Comeback
item.description: When Target Corp. named long-serving executive Michael Fiddelke to succeed Brian Cornell as chief executive officer a year ago, he had two tasks.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Felsted

item.title: Florida Primary Results: Democrats Make Things Harder for Themselves
item.description: Florida demonstrated on Tuesday that the Democratic Party’s identity crisis is alive and well. It’s the latest signal that while the midterm election will be a referendum on the president’s performance, it’s also a major test of the Democratic Party’s ability to bridge its growing divide.
item.dc:creator: Mary Ellen Klas

item.title: Mark Walter’s Lakers Sale Highlights Modern Sports Ownership Risks
item.description: Mark Walter should be precisely the kind of owner the National Basketball Association wants. He is spectacularly wealthy and — as he’s proved as the owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers — he’s willing to spend big to win.
item.dc:creator: Adam Minter

item.title: RFK Jr.’s Impact on Kindergarten Vaccine Rates Seen in CDC Data
item.description: In an early but damning gauge of Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s impact since his ascent to US health secretary, a growing number of Americans are sending their kids off to kindergarten without crucial vaccines.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Jarvis

item.title: The Decline in Murder Is Clear. The Reason Is Not
item.description: “Every single number is the lowest number in recorded history,” President Donald Trump said while unveiling the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s 2025 US crime report last week. It may not be surprising to learn that this was false: Despite falling sharply in 2025, the population-adjusted rate of aggravated assaults — one of the four main violent crimes tracked by the FBI — was still higher than in the early 2010s. item.dc:creator: Justin Fox

item.title: Malaria-Carrying Mosquitoes Have a New Foe in Science and Genetics
item.description: Almost half a million children under the age of 5 die of malaria each year. What if replacing a single amino acid in disease-carrying mosquitoes could help save them? After battling with rudimentary tools for millennia, malaria fighters are now armed with a potentially revolutionary technology. If only the public could get on board.
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: Apple Must Heed the Lessons of Meta’s ‘Pervert’ Glasses
item.description: In what looks like a curiously sloppy oversight, Apple Inc. has inadvertently confirmed Bloomberg’s reporting on the company’s first big swing at an AI-enhanced wearable device. Hidden in a coming Mac software update, a 13-second video shows a man wearing AirPods pick up a book and hold it in front of him. “With Visual Intelligence,” the voice-over says, “your world becomes savable. See something you like? Just ask me to save it for later.”
item.dc:creator: Dave Lee

item.title: Harvard Needs Honest Grading to Preserve Its Academic Credibility
item.description: University policies on grades, like grades themselves, run along a wide spectrum. Harvard, my alma mater and my employer, wants to combat grade inflation and so is limiting the number of A’s in undergraduate classes. Michigan, meanwhile, wants to combat grade anxiety and so is eliminating grades altogether for first-year students in their first semester.
item.dc:creator: Noah Feldman

item.title: The $19 Trillion Bond Question Confronting Central Banks
item.description: We all care about the interest rates that central banks set, but what about the $19 trillion of bonds and other assets held by the biggest among them? Those constitute a more esoteric, but equally consequential, element of monetary policy that’s lately transcended the wonky to become politically fractious.
